title: States and properties of matter; physical and chemical change
blurb: Classify matter, describe the states and phase changes, tell physical from chemical changes, calculate density and apply the basic gas laws.
question: An antacid tablet fizzes in a glass of water while an ice cube melts in another. Which change makes a new substance, which absorbs heat at a constant temperature, and how would you tell?

teach.body: Formally, matter is anything with mass that takes up space, made of particles in constant motion (kinetic molecular theory). A pure substance is an element (one kind of atom) or a compound (elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio, such as H₂O). A mixture is physically combined in any ratio. In plain English: a compound is a locked recipe; a mixture is a toss-together. Temperature measures the particles' average kinetic energy.

children.label: Element
children.sub: One kind of atom: Fe, O₂

teach.caption: Mixtures separate physically: filtration (solid from liquid), evaporation, distillation (by boiling point), chromatography, magnets. Milk is a colloid; muddy water is a suspension.
Plasma is an ionized gas (stars, lightning). Gases compress because their particles have lots of empty space between them.

head: Change
From → to
Heat
teach.caption: Toward gas absorbs heat; toward solid releases it. Dry ice sublimes; frost forms by deposition. Evaporating sweat absorbs heat, cooling the skin.
Plateaus: temperature holds during melting (0 °C) and boiling (100 °C) because the energy breaks attractions. Lower air pressure (high altitude) lowers the boiling point.
Bubbles in boiling water are water vapor: still H₂O, so boiling is physical. A precipitate forming from two clear solutions signals a reaction.

teach.body: A physical property is observed without changing what the substance is: color, density, melting and boiling point, hardness, solubility, conductivity. A chemical property describes how it reacts: flammability, reactivity with acid or oxygen, tendency to rust. Intensive properties do not depend on the amount (density, boiling point, temperature); extensive properties do (mass, volume).

Priya, a nursing applicant in her prerequisite lab, weighs a stone at 50 g. In a graduated cylinder the water rises from 30 mL to 50 mL, so its volume is 20 mL (water displacement). Density = mass ÷ volume = 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5 g/mL. That is more than water's 1.0 g/mL, so it sinks. Half the stone would still be 2.5 g/mL: density is intensive. Ice (about 0.92 g/cm³) floats.

head: Law
Held constant
Relationship
Example
teach.caption: Use kelvin in Charles's and Gay-Lussac's laws: K = °C + 273. Example: 6.0 L at 1.0 atm squeezed to 2.0 atm at constant T becomes 3.0 L.

teach.text: Dissolving and melting are PHYSICAL. Sublimation is solid → gas; deposition is gas → solid. Condensation and freezing RELEASE heat. Temperature does not rise during melting. Liquids DO have a definite volume. Density does NOT depend on sample size. Air is a mixture; water is a compound. And never put Celsius into Charles's law.

items: Elements and compounds are pure (compounds in a fixed ratio); mixtures vary and separate physically.
Solid: definite shape and volume. Liquid: definite volume only. Gas: neither, and compressible.
Melting, vaporization, sublimation absorb heat; freezing, condensation, deposition release it; temperature holds during each.
Physical change: same substance. Chemical change: new substance (gas, color change, precipitate, heat or light).
Density = mass ÷ volume (intensive). Boyle: P up, V down. Charles: T up, V up (kelvin).

summary: You can now classify matter as an element, compound or mixture, compare the states, name all six phase changes with their energy direction and read a heating curve. You can also tell physical from chemical properties and changes, calculate density from water displacement and apply Boyle's and Charles's laws.

A.q: Which state of matter has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container?
A.why: Liquid particles are close together (fixed volume) but slide past one another, so a liquid takes its container's shape.

whyNot.1: A solid keeps both its own shape and its volume.
whyNot.2: A gas has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume; it fills its container.
whyNot.3: Plasma is an ionized gas with no fixed shape or volume.

A.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
options: Ice cream melting in the sun
A.why: Rusting forms a new substance (iron oxide) with different properties, so it is a chemical change.

whyNot.0: Melting changes only the state; the ice cream is still the same substance.
whyNot.1: Dissolving sugar is physical: the sugar can be recovered by evaporating the water.
whyNot.2: Boiling turns liquid water into water vapor, the same substance in a different state.

A.q: Which phase change releases heat to the surroundings?
A.why: Condensation (gas to liquid) is exothermic: particles come together and release energy.

whyNot.0: Melting absorbs heat to separate particles in the solid.
whyNot.1: Sublimation absorbs heat to turn a solid directly into a gas.
whyNot.2: Vaporization absorbs heat (the heat of vaporization).

B.q: A 45 g sample has a volume of 15 mL. What is its density, and will it sink or float in water?
B.why: Density = 45 g ÷ 15 mL = 3.0 g/mL. That is greater than water's 1.0 g/mL, so it sinks.

whyNot.0: 0.33 g/mL divides volume by mass; density is mass ÷ volume.
whyNot.1: 3.0 g/mL is correct, but anything denser than water (1.0 g/mL) sinks.
whyNot.3: 675 multiplies mass by volume instead of dividing.

B.q: Which property stays the same no matter how much of a sample you have?
B.why: Boiling point is an intensive property: a drop and a pot of water boil at the same temperature.

whyNot.0: Mass is extensive: more sample, more mass.
whyNot.2: Volume is extensive and grows with the amount of sample.
whyNot.3: Total heat energy grows with the amount of sample, so it is extensive.

B.q: Ice at 0 °C is heated steadily on a hot plate. While the ice is melting, the thermometer reading:
options: climbs steadily as the ice melts
falls slightly as the ice melts
climbs once half the ice has melted
holds at 0 °C until it has melted
B.why: During a phase change the energy breaks attractions between particles, so temperature stays at the melting point until all the ice has melted.

whyNot.0: A steady climb happens only after melting is complete, when the liquid warms.
whyNot.1: Heat is being added, and melting absorbs it, so the temperature does not fall.
whyNot.2: The temperature stays flat for the whole plateau, not just the first half.

C.q: A 6.0 L sample of gas at 1.0 atm is compressed at constant temperature until its pressure is 3.0 atm. What is its new volume?
C.why: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, so 1.0 × 6.0 = 3.0 × V₂ and V₂ = 2.0 L. Tripling the pressure cuts the volume to one-third.

whyNot.0: 18 L treats pressure and volume as directly proportional; Boyle's law is inverse.
whyNot.1: 3.0 L halves the volume, but tripling the pressure cuts it to one-third.
whyNot.3: 0.50 L inverts the ratio (3.0 ÷ 6.0); the volume is 6.0 × (1.0 ÷ 3.0).

C.q: A sealed balloon at constant pressure is warmed from 27 °C to 54 °C. What happens to its volume?
options: It doubles, to twice the original
It stays at its starting size
C.why: Charles's law needs kelvin: 300 K → 327 K. V₂/V₁ = 327/300, about 1.09, so the volume rises by roughly one-tenth.

whyNot.0: Doubling uses the Celsius values directly; in kelvin the temperature rose only from 300 to 327.
whyNot.2: Heating a gas at constant pressure makes it expand, not shrink.
whyNot.3: Volume and kelvin temperature are directly proportional, so warming changes the volume.

C.q: A clear liquid is a uniform blend of ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) and water (100 °C). How is it best classified and separated?
options: A homogeneous mixture, separated by distillation
A heterogeneous mixture, separated by filtration
A homogeneous mixture, separated by filtration
C.why: The liquids are physically mixed in a uniform blend (a solution, homogeneous). Distillation separates liquids with different boiling points.

whyNot.0: Ethanol and water are not chemically combined in a fixed ratio, so the blend is not a compound.
whyNot.2: The blend is uniform, so it is homogeneous; filtration removes undissolved solids.
whyNot.3: Homogeneous is right, but dissolved liquids pass straight through a filter.

reteach.title: A school's three settings
reteach.question: Think about students in an exam hall, on a crowded dance floor and at recess on an open field. How do these match solids, liquids and gases, and what would a chemical change look like?

blocks.body: In the exam hall, students sit in fixed seats and only fidget: a solid. On the dance floor they are still close but move past each other: a liquid. At recess they run in every direction across the whole field: a gas. Energy moves them from one setting to the next, but they are the same students: a physical change. If two students left and came back as different people, that would be a chemical change.

blocks.text: Run the flow backward (freezing, condensing) and the energy is released, not absorbed. Every step in either direction is still physical: no new substance forms.

explain.body: Elements and compounds are pure substances; a compound's elements are chemically combined in a fixed ratio. Mixtures are physically combined in any ratio and can be homogeneous (uniform) or heterogeneous.

test.q: Which of these is a heterogeneous mixture?
test.why: Sand and water are not uniform: the sand is visible and settles, so the mixture is heterogeneous.

whyNot.0: Salt water is a solution, a homogeneous mixture that is uniform throughout.
whyNot.2: Air is a homogeneous mixture (a gas solution) of nitrogen, oxygen and other gases.
whyNot.3: Distilled water is a pure compound, not a mixture.

explain.body: Toward the gas state (melting, vaporization, sublimation) absorbs heat. Toward the solid state (condensation, freezing, deposition) releases heat. Temperature holds steady during each change.

test.q: Frost forms on a car windshield on a cold night as water vapor turns straight into ice. Which phase change is this?
test.why: Gas changing directly to solid is deposition.

whyNot.0: Sublimation is the reverse: solid directly to gas.
whyNot.1: Condensation is gas to liquid; frost skips the liquid stage.
whyNot.3: Freezing is liquid to solid; here the starting state is a gas.

explain.body: A physical change alters form or state but not identity. A chemical change makes a new substance, often shown by an unexpected gas, a color change, a precipitate, or heat and light.

test.q: Which of the following is a chemical property?
test.why: Flammability describes how a substance reacts (burns), which can be observed only by changing it chemically.

whyNot.0: Density is measured without changing the substance: a physical property.
whyNot.2: Boiling point is observed through a change of state, which is physical.
whyNot.3: Solubility is physical: dissolving does not create a new substance.

explain.body: Density = mass ÷ volume (g/mL or g/cm³; 1 mL = 1 cm³). Water is about 1.0 g/mL: denser objects sink, less dense ones float. Find an irregular solid's volume by water displacement.

test.q: A metal cube of mass 27 g is dropped into a graduated cylinder, and the water rises from 20 mL to 30 mL. What is the metal's density?
test.why: Volume = 30 − 20 = 10 mL. Density = 27 g ÷ 10 mL = 2.7 g/mL.

whyNot.0: 0.90 g/mL divides by the final reading (30 mL) instead of the volume displaced.
whyNot.1: 1.35 g/mL divides by the starting reading (20 mL) instead of the volume displaced.
whyNot.3: 0.37 g/mL divides volume by mass (10 ÷ 27); density is mass ÷ volume.
